author: Joseph Volpe Sun staff writer
title: Charlestown becomes second R.I. town to ban data centers | Daily-news-alerts | thewesterlysun.com
text:
CHARLESTOWN — The Town Council voted 5-0 Tuesday to prohibit Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and data centers in Charlestown, while directing town officials to clarify the ordinance’s language regarding residential battery systems.
Councilor Bonnie Van Slyke, the sponsor of the agenda item, said that both BESS and data centers are currently considered non-permitted uses because they are not included in the town’s use table.
“Both of them relate to the fact that Charlestown is entirely dependent on well water and septic systems. The battery storage has the issue of potentially causing fires and also leaking fluids, with the possibility of groundwater contamination,” she said. “Data centers gobble up the land and they use a lot of electricity and water. They’re something that we should be looking at very carefully.”
There are currently no plans to have a data center constructed in Charlestown, and town officials are passing this ordinance as a preventative measure for possible future data center development, as well as BESS.
The Town Council opened the public hearing, but no residents signed up to speak or spoke during the hearing
Town Council President Deborah Carney said they have received an opinion from the Planning Commission, saying that they agree with the council's decision to go forward and implement the ordinance prohibiting BESS and data centers. According to her, the commission said that the ordinance was “consistent with the comprehensive plan, and the principals of the Charlestown zoning ordinance.”
Van Slyke said a concern of some residents was those who had batteries attached to solar panels on their houses. She said that, according to Building/Zoning Official Joseph Warner, those systems are a consumer product intended for individual use and would be covered by the exemptions in the ordinance.
Councilor Stephen Stokes brought up concerns about how the definition of BESS is worded in the ordinance, saying that it conflicts with existing battery systems that are intended for individual use, such as solar panels.
“If I have solar panels and I have a battery bank, that meets this definition in the ordinance. Obviously, we don’t want commercialized battery storage facilities, but this is defining energy storage systems,” he said.
Town Solicitor Peter Ruggiero suggested that Warner should be consulted for including appropriate language that would more specifically define what is allowed for use in terms of BESS.
Planning Commission Chair Ruth Platner added that the town currently has a prohibition on the commercial production of electricity, which would protect individuals that use energy storage systems.
“I think as long as we have that prohibition, people will not be producing more electricity than someone is storing from their rooftop solar panel systems,” she said.
The council voted 5-0 to pass the ordinance prohibiting BESS and data centers. Stokes made an additional motion that passed, which was to send the ordinance to Ruggiero and Warner to clean up the language for BESS in order to have a more solid definition of what is prohibited and what is not.
Charlestown is now the second town in the state to officially prohibit data centers, with the first being Smithfield.
In the draft ordinance language, BESS is defined as a large battery system that stores electricity so it can be used later. Unlike household batteries or electric vehicle batteries, these systems are designed to store energy for homes, businesses or the electric grid.
Wording in the ordinance also denotes the prohibited use of Battery Storage Management Systems, which is a built-in safety system that monitors a battery storage system and automatically shuts it down or puts it into a safe mode if it detects dangerous conditions, such as overheating.
Smithfield passed an ordinance banning the use of data centers on May 5. In that ordinance, data centers are defined as a building or complex designed primarily to house computer servers and other equipment that stores, processes and transmits digital data. These facilities support services such as cloud computing, artificial intelligence and large-scale data storage, and are significantly larger than the computer systems found in typical offices or businesses.
Neighboring communities such as Hopkinton have also been discussing options to prohibit data centers, as on July 6, the Hopkinton Town Council voted to direct Hopkinton's Planning Board and Planning Department to study and recommend an ordinance that would ban data centers in town.
summary: Councilor Bonnie Van Slyke, the sponsor of the agenda item, said that both BESS and data centers are currently considered non-permitted uses because they are not included in the town’s use table. According to her, the commission said that the ordinance was “consistent with the comprehensive plan, and the principals of the Charlestown zoning ordinance.” Van Slyke said a concern of some residents was those who had batteries attached to solar panels on their houses.
